title: Rudra, the one god
hookLine: the wild storm god of the Vedas becomes, in the Shvetashvatara, the one Lord who rules every world
carry: god is one, with no second
tomorrow: smaller than small, greater than great
last: YOGA IS THE BOAT TO BRAHMAN.

cards: In the Rig Veda, Rudra is the god you'd rather keep at a distance. He's an archer, linked with storms and wild places. The hymns ask him, more than once, to spare their children and their cattle.
Yet the same hymns call him a healer, the best of physicians, with soothing remedies in his hand. Terrifying and tender in one figure, belonging to the edges, the wild places beyond the village.
Then the Shvetashvatara picks him up and puts him at the center of everything.

teach.b: Chapter three opens with a figure who holds a net and rules with his powers. Then verse 3.2, in paraphrase: Rudra is truly one; they do not stand for a second. He rules all these worlds with his powers.
He stands within every creature, and at the end of time he draws the worlds back in, the one who made them and protects them.
Verse 3.3 widens the picture to fill the sky: eyes everywhere, faces everywhere, arms everywhere, feet everywhere, the one God who forges heaven and earth.
And 3.4 calls Rudra the source of the gods. Earlier this year, the Upanishads often spoke of Brahman in impersonal words: being, consciousness, not this, not this.

The Shvetashvatara gives that reality a face and a name, a Lord, Ishvara, whom you can turn toward. A few verses later it asks him to show his kind, auspicious form, and the word for auspicious is shiva.
That's one reason Shaiva readers prize this Upanishad.
Here's the teaching, plainly: Hindus worship many forms, and many Hindus understand them as faces of one God, the source of all the gods, one with no second.
So when someone asks how many gods Hindus have, this text gives an old answer: one, with many faces. A family pouring water over a Shiva linga on a Monday is turning toward that One.

how: Many Shaiva Hindus honor Rudra-Shiva in daily worship, some by chanting the Shri Rudram from the Yajur Veda and offering water to the Shiva linga, and Shaiva teachers often turn to the Shvetashvatara as a key scripture.

o: a gentle goddess of rivers and healing
a fierce demon the gods had to defeat
the storm god and healer, called the one Lord

games.q: Rudra across the texts: tap the pairs.
p: archer of the storm, and a healer

s: in the Vedas Rudra is only a destroyer
the hymns fear him, but also call him a healer with soothing remedies.
the Shvetashvatara calls Rudra one, with no second
verse 3.2: he rules all the worlds with his powers.
the word shiva means auspicious or kind
the Upanishad asks Rudra to show his shiva form, his kind one.

games.q: a classmate says Hindus have millions of gods and none of them is in charge. what does the Shvetashvatara's chapter three say?
o: right: many equal gods and no one source.
Rudra is one with no second, the source of the gods: many faces, one God.
there are no gods at all, only an impersonal force.
games.why: 3.2 calls Rudra one, with no second, ruling all the worlds; 3.4 calls him the source of the gods. a personal God you can turn toward.

practice: Sit in yesterday's posture and take verse 3.3 slowly: eyes everywhere, so you're seen, not judged; faces everywhere, the faces you passed today; hands and feet everywhere, the air on your skin, the ground holding you.
If you pray, rest in the thought of the one who rules; if not, rest in the plain feel of the ground and the air.

wordCard.voice: Rudra. The fierce and healing god of the Vedas, whom the Shvetashvatara calls the one Lord, with no second, ruling every world.

orig.note: Sanskrit rudra: the Vedic god often linked with storms and healing; in the Shvetashvatara, the one Lord.

carryVoice: Your line: God is one, with no second. Storm and healer, source of the gods. Day four hundred twenty-six.
